answer.worked: The range of $f$ is $(0,1]$, so the domain of $f^{-1}$ is $(0,1]$.

$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{1}{1+y^2}\\x(1+y^2)&=1\\xy^2&=1-x\\y^2&=\frac{1-x}{x}\\y&=\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{x}}\end{align*}$$
Take the positive branch because $y\geq0$. Thus $f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{\dfrac{1-x}{x}}$, with $0<x\leq1$.

inlines.text: is a root of the equation

answer.worked:
Let $P=(\alpha,\beta)$. Since $P$ lies on $y=f(x)$, $\beta=\dfrac{1}{1+\alpha^2}$. Since $P$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$, $f^{-1}(\alpha)=\beta$, so $f(\beta)=\alpha$, that is $\alpha=\dfrac{1}{1+\beta^2}$.

Subtract to show $\alpha=\beta$:
$$\begin{align*}\beta-\alpha&=\frac{1}{1+\alpha^2}-\frac{1}{1+\beta^2}\\&=\frac{\beta^2-\alpha^2}{(1+\alpha^2)(1+\beta^2)}.\end{align*}$$
If $\alpha\neq\beta$, divide by $\beta-\alpha$ to get $(1+\alpha^2)(1+\beta^2)=\alpha+\beta$. But
$$\begin{align*}(1+\alpha^2)(1+\beta^2)&\geq1+\alpha^2+\beta^2\\1+\alpha^2+\beta^2-(\alpha+\beta)&=\left(\alpha-\tfrac12\right)^2+\left(\beta-\tfrac12\right)^2+\tfrac12>0,\end{align*}$$
so $(1+\alpha^2)(1+\beta^2)>\alpha+\beta$, a contradiction. Hence $\alpha=\beta$, so $P$ lies on $y=x$.

Then $\alpha=f(\alpha)$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{1+\alpha^2}&=\alpha\\1&=\alpha(1+\alpha^2)\\1&=\alpha+\alpha^3\\\alpha^3+\alpha-1&=0\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\alpha$ is a root of $x^3+x-1=0$.
